claim: Brazil has experienced over 22 million COVID-19 cases and 621,000 deaths as of 14 January 2022.
source: Brazil has experienced one of the world's most significant COVID-19 epidemics, with over 22 million cases and 621,000 deaths reported as of 14 January 2022.
evidence: Direct statement of reported case and death counts from official data as of a specific date.

claim: There is extensive variation in SARS-CoV-2 spread between population groups in Brazil.
source: However, this national picture masks important sub-national heterogeneity, with extensive variation in SARS-CoV-2 spread between population groups (Li et al., 2021) and locations (Castro et al., 2021; Hallal et al., 2020) as well as regional differences in the stringency of non-pharmaceutical interventions (de Souza Santos et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies documenting heterogeneity in spread.

claim: There is extensive variation in SARS-CoV-2 spread between locations in Brazil.
source: However, this national picture masks important sub-national heterogeneity, with extensive variation in SARS-CoV-2 spread between population groups (Li et al., 2021) and locations (Castro et al., 2021; Hallal et al., 2020) as well as regional differences in the stringency of non-pharmaceutical interventions (de Souza Santos et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies documenting geographic heterogeneity.

claim: There are regional differences in the stringency of non-pharmaceutical interventions in Brazil.
source: However, this national picture masks important sub-national heterogeneity, with extensive variation in SARS-CoV-2 spread between population groups (Li et al., 2021) and locations (Castro et al., 2021; Hallal et al., 2020) as well as regional differences in the stringency of non-pharmaceutical interventions (de Souza Santos et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published study on intervention stringency.

claim: The Gamma (P.1) variant of concern emerged in November 2020.
source: Indeed, a significant fraction of the COVID-19 burden in Brazil was driven by the emergence of the Gamma (P.1) variant of concern (VOC) in November 2020, which drove extensive resurgence of transmission following its apparent emergence in the Amazonas State capital city of Manaus.
evidence: Direct statement of the timing of Gamma variant emergence.

claim: The Gamma variant emerged in Manaus.
source: Indeed, a significant fraction of the COVID-19 burden in Brazil was driven by the emergence of the Gamma (P.1) variant of concern (VOC) in November 2020, which drove extensive resurgence of transmission following its apparent emergence in the Amazonas State capital city of Manaus.
evidence: Direct statement of the geographic origin of the Gamma variant.

claim: The Gamma variant drove extensive resurgence of transmission in Manaus despite evidence of high levels of population-level immunity.
source: Indeed, a significant fraction of the COVID-19 burden in Brazil was driven by the emergence of the Gamma (P.1) variant of concern (VOC) in November 2020, which drove extensive resurgence of transmission following its apparent emergence in the Amazonas State capital city of Manaus. Despite the evidence of high levels of population-level immunity that should have hindered further transmission (Buss et al., 2021), a phenomenon attributed to the Gamma VOCs likely increased transmissibility and ability to partially evade immune responses (Faria et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies documenting high immunity levels and Gamma's properties.

claim: The Gamma variant has likely increased transmissibility.
source: Despite the evidence of high levels of population-level immunity that should have hindered further transmission (Buss et al., 2021), a phenomenon attributed to the Gamma VOCs likely increased transmissibility and ability to partially evade immune responses (Faria et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published study on Gamma variant properties.

claim: The Gamma variant has the ability to partially evade immune responses.
source: Despite the evidence of high levels of population-level immunity that should have hindered further transmission (Buss et al., 2021), a phenomenon attributed to the Gamma VOCs likely increased transmissibility and ability to partially evade immune responses (Faria et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published study on Gamma variant immune evasion.

claim: Subsequent spread of Gamma to the rest of Brazil led to resurgence, extensive transmission, and disease burden leading to substantial pressure on health systems.
source: Subsequent spread to the rest of Brazil led to similar resurgence, extensive transmission, and disease burden leading to substantial pressure on health systems (Brizzi et al., 2021; de Oliveira et al., 2021; Martins et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies documenting health system impacts.

claim: Previous natural infection may enhance vaccine response.
source: More generally, because previous natural infection may enhance vaccine response (Crotty, 2021; Reynolds et al., 2021; Stamatatos et al., 2021), understanding the extent of previous exposure in the country may have important implications for the development of epidemic waves driven by new variants in the context of the ongoing large-scale, nationwide vaccination campaign.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on vaccine response enhancement.

claim: The study analyzed SARS-CoV-2 dynamics in eight of the biggest Brazilian cities: Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, Fortaleza, Manaus, Recife, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador, and São Paulo.
source: Here, we analyse the divergent epidemic SARS-CoV-2 dynamics in eight of the biggest Brazilian cities (Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, Fortaleza, Manaus, Recife, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador, and São Paulo).
evidence: Direct statement of the study locations.

claim: The study tested 97,950 blood donation samples for IgG antibodies from March 2020 to March 2021.
source: We tested 97,950 blood donation samples for IgG antibodies from March 2020 to March 2021 in 8 of Brazil's most populous cities.
evidence: Direct statement of sample size and study period from the abstract.

claim: The inferred attack rate of SARS-CoV-2 in December 2020 in Curitiba was 19.3% (95% credible interval 17.5–21.2%).
source: The inferred attack rate of SARS-CoV-2 in December 2020, before the Gamma variant of concern (VOC) was dominant, ranged from 19.3% (95% credible interval [CrI] 17.5–21.2%) in Curitiba to 75.0% (95% CrI 70.8–80.3%) in Manaus.
evidence: Direct statement of estimated attack rate with credible intervals from the abstract.

claim: The inferred attack rate of SARS-CoV-2 in December 2020 in Manaus was 75.0% (95% credible interval 70.8–80.3%).
source: The inferred attack rate of SARS-CoV-2 in December 2020, before the Gamma variant of concern (VOC) was dominant, ranged from 19.3% (95% credible interval [CrI] 17.5–21.2%) in Curitiba to 75.0% (95% CrI 70.8–80.3%) in Manaus.
evidence: Direct statement of estimated attack rate with credible intervals from the abstract.

claim: Seroprevalence was consistently smaller in women.
source: Seroprevalence was consistently smaller in women and donors older than 55 years.
evidence: Direct statement of demographic pattern in seroprevalence from the abstract.

claim: Seroprevalence was consistently smaller in donors older than 55 years.
source: Seroprevalence was consistently smaller in women and donors older than 55 years.
evidence: Direct statement of demographic pattern in seroprevalence from the abstract.

claim: The age-specific infection fatality rate differed between cities.
source: The age-specific infection fatality rate (IFR) differed between cities and consistently increased with age.
evidence: Direct statement of IFR variation from the abstract.

claim: The age-specific infection fatality rate consistently increased with age.
source: The age-specific infection fatality rate (IFR) differed between cities and consistently increased with age.
evidence: Direct statement of age-dependent IFR pattern from the abstract.

claim: The infection hospitalisation rate increased significantly during the Gamma-dominated second wave in Manaus.
source: The infection hospitalisation rate increased significantly during the Gamma-dominated second wave in Manaus, suggesting increased morbidity of the Gamma VOC compared to previous variants circulating in Manaus.
evidence: Direct statement of IHR increase with inference about Gamma morbidity from the abstract.

claim: The Gamma variant has increased morbidity compared to previous variants circulating in Manaus.
source: The infection hospitalisation rate increased significantly during the Gamma-dominated second wave in Manaus, suggesting increased morbidity of the Gamma VOC compared to previous variants circulating in Manaus.
evidence: Inference based on observed IHR increase during Gamma-dominated period.

claim: The higher disease penetrance associated with the health system's collapse increased the overall IFR by a minimum factor of 2.91 (95% CrI 2.43–3.53).
source: The higher disease penetrance associated with the health system's collapse increased the overall IFR by a minimum factor of 2.91 (95% CrI 2.43–3.53).
evidence: Direct statement of IFR increase with credible intervals from the abstract.

claim: Each of the eight cities had a monthly quota of 1,000 kits for testing selected donation samples.
source: Each of the eight cities had a monthly quota of 1,000 kits for testing selected donation samples in this study.
evidence: Direct statement of sampling design from Methods section.

claim: Blood samples were selected so that the spatial distribution of residential location of selected donors matches the spatial distribution of population density in each municipality.
source: In order to select more representative samples, we selected blood samples so that the spatial distribution of residential location of selected donors matches the spatial distribution of population density in each municipality.
evidence: Direct statement of sampling strategy from Methods section.

claim: In Manaus, donor postcodes were not reliably collected, so samples were selected consecutively with no postal code restrictions.
source: In Manaus, however, donor postcodes were not reliably collected, so that the number of missing and wrong values makes this strategy unfeasible. So, samples were selected consecutively with no postal code restrictions.
evidence: Direct statement of sampling limitation and alternative approach in Manaus.

claim: From 453,211 available blood samples collected in all 8 cities except Manaus, 72,783 had a missing or invalid residential postal code.
source: From 453,211 available blood samples collected in all 8 cities except Manaus, 72,783 had a missing or invalid residential postal code, and 198,199 were from individuals living in regions not included in this study, thus 182,229 samples were eligible for selection.
evidence: Direct statement of sample exclusion criteria and numbers from Methods section.

claim: 198,199 samples were from individuals living in regions not included in the study.
source: From 453,211 available blood samples collected in all 8 cities except Manaus, 72,783 had a missing or invalid residential postal code, and 198,199 were from individuals living in regions not included in this study, thus 182,229 samples were eligible for selection.
evidence: Direct statement of sample exclusion criteria and numbers from Methods section.

claim: 182,229 samples were eligible for selection.
source: From 453,211 available blood samples collected in all 8 cities except Manaus, 72,783 had a missing or invalid residential postal code, and 198,199 were from individuals living in regions not included in this study, thus 182,229 samples were eligible for selection.
evidence: Direct statement of eligible sample size from Methods section.

claim: An average of 1010 samples were selected monthly for each city from March 2020 to March 2021, except for Recife where tests occurred until February 2021.
source: An average of 1010 samples were selected monthly for each city from March 2020 to March 2021, except for Recife where tests occurred until February 2021.
evidence: Direct statement of sampling frequency and duration from Methods section.

claim: A total of 104,013 samples were selected, but 6063 samples could not be retrieved or did not have enough volume to be tested, leading to 97,950 tested samples.
source: A total of 104,013 samples were selected, but 6063 samples could not be retrieved or did not have enough volume to be tested, leading to 97,950 tested samples (951 samples per month in average for each city).
evidence: Direct statement of final sample size and exclusions from Methods section.

claim: In Brazil, blood donation samples are usually saved for 6 months.
source: In Brazil, blood donation samples are usually saved for 6 months, so when serological test kits were made available in July 2020, we could retrospectively select and test frozen samples from February to July.
evidence: Direct statement of sample storage practice from Methods section.

claim: Antibody tests results were not made available to the blood donors themselves.
source: Antibody tests results were not made available to the blood donors themselves.
evidence: Direct statement of study protocol from Methods section.

claim: Blood donors differ systematically in age, sex, and self-reported skin colour compared to the population.
source: Donors differ systematically in age, sex, and self-reported skin colour compared to the population, but the income per capita is similar.
evidence: Statement based on comparison with census data, referencing Appendix figures.

claim: The income per capita of blood donors is similar to the general population.
source: Donors differ systematically in age, sex, and self-reported skin colour compared to the population, but the income per capita is similar.
evidence: Statement based on comparison with census data, referencing Appendix figures.

claim: The study applied chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassays (CIMA, AdviseDx, Abbott) that detect IgG antibodies against the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N).
source: We applied chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassays (CIMA, AdviseDx, Abbott) that detect IgG antibodies against the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) because it was the only automated commercially available kit in Brazil when the study started (July 2020).
evidence: Direct statement of assay type and rationale from Methods section.

claim: The Abbott anti-N IgG CMIA was the only automated commercially available kit in Brazil when the study started in July 2020.
source: We applied chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassays (CIMA, AdviseDx, Abbott) that detect IgG antibodies against the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) because it was the only automated commercially available kit in Brazil when the study started (July 2020).
evidence: Direct statement of kit availability from Methods section.

claim: The Abbott anti-N IgG CMIA shows particularly rapid signal decay when compared with other assays.
source: The Abbott anti-N IgG CMIA shows particularly rapid signal decay when compared with other assays (Di Germanio et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published study on assay characteristics.

claim: A test is considered positive if the obtained signal to cutoff (S/C) is greater or equal to 0.49.
source: A test is considered positive if the obtained signal to cutoff (S/C) is greater or equal to a predefined threshold of 0.49.
evidence: Direct statement of test positivity threshold from Methods section.

claim: The threshold of 0.49 is the lower threshold recommended by the manufacturer.
source: This is the lower threshold recommended by the manufacturer, which was used instead of the upper threshold of 1.4 to partially attenuate the effect of seroreversion.
evidence: Direct statement of manufacturer recommendation and rationale from Methods section.

claim: The sensitivity of the anti-N assay using a threshold of 0.49 S/C was 90.6%.
source: We found a sensitivity of 90.6% for the anti-N assay using a threshold of 0.49 S/C and 94.0% for the anti-S assay.
evidence: Direct statement of assay sensitivity from Methods section based on validation cohort.

claim: The sensitivity of the anti-S assay was 94.0%.
source: We found a sensitivity of 90.6% for the anti-N assay using a threshold of 0.49 S/C and 94.0% for the anti-S assay.
evidence: Direct statement of assay sensitivity from Methods section based on validation cohort.

claim: Specificity for the anti-N assay was 97.5%, with 801 negative results in 821 pre-pandemic blood donation samples.
source: Specificity for the anti-N assay was 97.5%, with 801 negative results in 821 pre-pandemic blood donation samples (Buss et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct statement of assay specificity with supporting data and citation.

claim: The anti-S assay has a specificity of >99%.
source: The anti-S assay has a specificity of >99% (Di Germanio et al., 2021; Stone et al., 2021), and we assume 100% in this study.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on assay specificity.

claim: The sensitivity of both anti-N and anti-S assays declines through time due to waning of the detected antibodies below the positivity threshold.
source: Although the sensitivity of both assays declines through time due to waning of the detected antibodies below the positivity threshold, the anti-S IgG antibodies wane more slowly (Di Germanio et al., 2021; Stone et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on antibody waning kinetics.

claim: The anti-S IgG antibodies wane more slowly than anti-N IgG antibodies.
source: Although the sensitivity of both assays declines through time due to waning of the detected antibodies below the positivity threshold, the anti-S IgG antibodies wane more slowly (Di Germanio et al., 2021; Stone et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on antibody waning kinetics.

claim: Sensitivity obtained from convalescent plasma donors is likely overestimated due to spectrum bias.
source: Sensitivity obtained from convalescent plasma donors is likely overestimated due to spectrum bias. This is because convalescent donors had moderate-to-severe SARS-CoV-2 infection, and thus differ from the whole blood donor population (used to estimate seroprevalence), who are more likely to have had asymptomatic or mild disease.
evidence: Inference based on known differences between convalescent plasma donors and whole blood donors.

claim: Convalescent donors had moderate-to-severe SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: This is because convalescent donors had moderate-to-severe SARS-CoV-2 infection, and thus differ from the whole blood donor population (used to estimate seroprevalence), who are more likely to have had asymptomatic or mild disease.
evidence: Direct statement about disease severity in convalescent donors from Methods section.

claim: Whole blood donors are more likely to have had asymptomatic or mild disease.
source: This is because convalescent donors had moderate-to-severe SARS-CoV-2 infection, and thus differ from the whole blood donor population (used to estimate seroprevalence), who are more likely to have had asymptomatic or mild disease.
evidence: Inference based on blood donation eligibility criteria.

claim: 7675 repeat whole blood donors in Manaus were identified and tested who had made multiple donations throughout 2020–2021.
source: We identified and tested 7675 repeat whole blood donors in Manaus who had made multiple donations throughout for 2020–2021 (Appendix 1—figure 14) and used these data to estimate the time-to-seroreversion probability distribution (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct statement of repeat donor cohort size from Results section.

claim: Repeat blood donors had a shorter assay signal half-life than plasma donors (median [IQR] 69.3 [53.0–103.8] versus 105.9 [62.7–185.1] days).
source: Repeat blood donors had a shorter assay signal half-life than plasma donors (median [IQR] 69.3 [53.0–103.8] versus 105.9 [62.7–185.1] days) and a lower observed peak S/C ratio (median [IQR] 2.89 [1.49–4.83] versus 5.08 [3.22–6.99]), yielding a shorter median time between seroconversion and seroreversion (203 [147–294] days versus 280 [175–441] days).
evidence: Direct statement of measured half-life with statistical summaries from Results section and Figure 1.

claim: Repeat blood donors had a lower observed peak S/C ratio than plasma donors (median [IQR] 2.89 [1.49–4.83] versus 5.08 [3.22–6.99]).
source: Repeat blood donors had a shorter assay signal half-life than plasma donors (median [IQR] 69.3 [53.0–103.8] versus 105.9 [62.7–185.1] days) and a lower observed peak S/C ratio (median [IQR] 2.89 [1.49–4.83] versus 5.08 [3.22–6.99]), yielding a shorter median time between seroconversion and seroreversion (203 [147–294] days versus 280 [175–441] days).
evidence: Direct statement of measured peak S/C with statistical summaries from Results section and Figure 1.

claim: Repeat blood donors had a shorter median time between seroconversion and seroreversion than plasma donors (203 [147–294] days versus 280 [175–441] days).
source: Repeat blood donors had a shorter assay signal half-life than plasma donors (median [IQR] 69.3 [53.0–103.8] versus 105.9 [62.7–185.1] days) and a lower observed peak S/C ratio (median [IQR] 2.89 [1.49–4.83] versus 5.08 [3.22–6.99]), yielding a shorter median time between seroconversion and seroreversion (203 [147–294] days versus 280 [175–441] days).
evidence: Direct statement of calculated time to seroreversion with statistical summaries from Results section and Figure 1.

claim: The eight Brazilian state capitals collectively represent approximately 14% of the total Brazilian population.
source: They collectively represent approximately 14% of the total Brazilian population.
evidence: Direct statement of population representation from Results section.

claim: Between 1 March 2020 and 31 March 2021, the age-standardised mortality rate varied from 1.7 deaths per 1,000 inhabitants in Belo Horizonte to 5.3 deaths per 1,000 in Manaus.
source: Between 1 March 2020 and 31 March 2021, the age-standardised mortality rate varied from 1.7 deaths per 1,000 inhabitants in Belo Horizonte to 5.3 deaths per 1,000 in Manaus, which had twice the mortality of Fortaleza, the city with the next highest mortality (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct statement of mortality rates with reference to Figure 2C from Results section.

claim: Manaus had twice the mortality of Fortaleza, the city with the next highest mortality.
source: Between 1 March 2020 and 31 March 2021, the age-standardised mortality rate varied from 1.7 deaths per 1,000 inhabitants in Belo Horizonte to 5.3 deaths per 1,000 in Manaus, which had twice the mortality of Fortaleza, the city with the next highest mortality (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct statement of relative mortality with reference to Figure 2C from Results section.

claim: Manaus returned to pre-pandemic levels of mobility by July 2020.
source: Manaus, the city with the youngest population, returned to pre-pandemic levels of mobility by July 2020, having consistently lower homestay index (i.e. higher mobility) than other cities after June 2020, whereas the other seven cities showed a relatively homogenous mobility pattern.
evidence: Direct statement based on homestay index data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Manaus had consistently lower homestay index (i.e. higher mobility) than other cities after June 2020.
source: Manaus, the city with the youngest population, returned to pre-pandemic levels of mobility by July 2020, having consistently lower homestay index (i.e. higher mobility) than other cities after June 2020, whereas the other seven cities showed a relatively homogenous mobility pattern.
evidence: Direct statement based on homestay index data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Manaus is the city with the youngest population among the eight studied cities.
source: Manaus, the city with the youngest population, returned to pre-pandemic levels of mobility by July 2020, having consistently lower homestay index (i.e. higher mobility) than other cities after June 2020, whereas the other seven cities showed a relatively homogenous mobility pattern.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing age distributions.

claim: Manaus had the lowest income per capita among the eight cities.
source: Manaus was also an outlier in having the lowest income per capita, health insurance coverage, and lowest proportion of the population with comorbidities, along with the highest number of residents per household (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2 from Results section.

claim: Manaus had the lowest health insurance coverage among the eight cities.
source: Manaus was also an outlier in having the lowest income per capita, health insurance coverage, and lowest proportion of the population with comorbidities, along with the highest number of residents per household (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2 from Results section.

claim: Manaus had the lowest proportion of the population with comorbidities among the eight cities.
source: Manaus was also an outlier in having the lowest income per capita, health insurance coverage, and lowest proportion of the population with comorbidities, along with the highest number of residents per household (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2 from Results section.

claim: Manaus had the highest number of residents per household among the eight cities.
source: Manaus was also an outlier in having the lowest income per capita, health insurance coverage, and lowest proportion of the population with comorbidities, along with the highest number of residents per household (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2 from Results section.

claim: Men tended to have higher attack rates than women across the eight cities.
source: Across the eight cities, our results consistently show differences between sexes - on average, men tended to have higher attack rates than women, although the degree and extent of this difference varied between cities.
evidence: Direct statement based on seroprevalence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In São Paulo, the seroprevalence in December 2020 for men was 30.6% compared to 23.0% estimated in women (i.e. 33.5% (95% CrI 17.7–51.9) higher).
source: In São Paulo, the seroprevalence in December 2020 for men was 30.6% compared to the 23.0% estimated in women (i.e. 33.5% (95% CrI 17.7–51.9) higher, Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement of sex-specific seroprevalence with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: In Curitiba, seroprevalence in December 2020 was similar for women and men, being only 4.65% (95% CrI –11.5 to 18.5) higher in women.
source: By contrast, seroprevalence in Curitiba in December 2020 was similar for women and men, being only 4.65% (95% CrI –11.5 to 18.5) higher in women.
evidence: Direct statement of sex-specific seroprevalence comparison from Results section.

claim: Seroprevalence in December 2020 was typically highest in younger age groups.
source: We also observed an extensive variation in the dynamics of population-level seroprevalence between age groups, with seroprevalence in December 2020 typically highest in younger age groups.
evidence: Direct statement based on age-stratified seroprevalence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The seroprevalence of individuals below the age of 55 increased in all cities except for Recife when compared to donors aged between 55 and 69.
source: The seroprevalence of individuals below the age of 55 increased in all cities except for Recife when compared to donors aged between 55 and 69, increasing by 34.1% (95% CrI –2.23–91.2) in Curitiba and decreasing by a small factor of 0.5% (95% CrI –24.8–19.1) in Recife.
evidence: Direct statement of age-specific seroprevalence patterns from Results section.

claim: In cities with a large increase in seroprevalence during the first epidemic wave (i.e. Manaus, Recife, Fortaleza, and Salvador), this was primarily driven by younger men.
source: Furthermore, in cities with a large increase in seroprevalence during the first epidemic wave (i.e. Manaus, Recife, Fortaleza, and Salvador), this was primarily driven by younger men.
evidence: Direct statement based on age-sex stratified seroprevalence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Manaus, seroprevalence was significantly larger in men and younger individuals aged 16–44 in July 2020.
source: In Manaus, seroprevalence was significantly larger in men and younger individuals aged 16–44 in July 2020, but between July and December seroprevalence increased faster in women and donors older than 45 years, leading to smaller differences in attack rate by age and sex in December 2020 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement based on temporal changes in age-sex stratified seroprevalence shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Between July and December 2020 in Manaus, seroprevalence increased faster in women and donors older than 45 years.
source: In Manaus, seroprevalence was significantly larger in men and younger individuals aged 16–44 in July 2020, but between July and December seroprevalence increased faster in women and donors older than 45 years, leading to smaller differences in attack rate by age and sex in December 2020 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement based on temporal changes in age-sex stratified seroprevalence shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The IFR significantly increases with age, ranging from 0.03% in individuals aged 16–24 years to 1.31% in individuals aged 55–64 years.
source: Our results show the IFR significantly increases with age, ranging from 0.03% in individuals aged 16–24 years to 1.31% in individuals aged 55–64 years.
evidence: Direct statement of age-specific IFR estimates with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Cities presented different age-standardised overall IFRs, being smaller in Manaus (0.24%) and higher in Curitiba (0.54%).
source: Cities presented different age-standardised overall IFRs, being smaller in Manaus (0.24%) and higher in Curitiba (0.54%).
evidence: Direct statement of city-specific overall IFR estimates from Results section.

claim: There was a strong correlation (Pearson's correlation = 0.92) between the age-standardised mortality rate in each city and the attack rate inferred from blood donor serosurveillance data.
source: There was a strong correlation (Pearson's correlation = 0.92) between the age-standardised mortality rate in each city and the attack rate inferred from blood donor serosurveillance data (Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The obtained age-specific IFRs were similar to the estimates from Brazeau et al., 2020.
source: Despite the differences between cities, the obtained age-specific IFRs were similar to the estimates from Brazeau et al., 2020 but higher than the estimates from O'Driscoll et al., 2021 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Direct comparison with published IFR estimates shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The obtained age-specific IFRs were higher than the estimates from O'Driscoll et al., 2021.
source: Despite the differences between cities, the obtained age-specific IFRs were similar to the estimates from Brazeau et al., 2020 but higher than the estimates from O'Driscoll et al., 2021 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Direct comparison with published IFR estimates shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The estimated upper bound for the age-standardised cumulative attack rate in the Gamma-dominated period in Manaus was 37.5% (95% CrI 35.3–42.6).
source: The estimated upper bound for the age-standardised cumulative attack rate in the second period dominated by the Gamma variant was 37.5% (95% CrI 35.3–42.6), significantly smaller than the cumulative attack rate of 75.0% (Figure 2) estimated for the first period dominated by non-Gamma variants.
evidence: Direct statement of estimated attack rate upper bound from Results section.

claim: The lower bound for the IHR increased in all age groups during the Gamma-dominated period in Manaus, from 34.4% (95% CrI 6.5–70.0) in individuals aged 16–24 to 163.4% (95% CrI 90.9–264.3) in individuals aged 45–54 when compared to the IHR estimated for the non-Gamma period.
source: The lower bound for the IHR increased in all age groups, from 34.4% (95% CrI 6.5–70.0) in individuals aged 16–24 to 163.4% (95% CrI 90.9–264.3) in individuals aged 45–54 when compared to the IHR estimated for the non-Gamma period.
evidence: Direct statement of IHR increase with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The age-specific IFR increased during the Gamma-dominated period in Manaus, with a lower bound increasing 93.8% (95% CrI 36.4–186.4) in individuals aged 55–64 to 273.5% (95% CrI 167.8–423.4%) in individuals aged 45–54 when compared to the first wave.
source: The increased hospitalisation risk combined with an increased in-hospital fatality rate (HFR, defined as the number of deaths per hospitalisation) during the second wave (Appendix 1—figure 19) resulted in an increased age-specific IFR, with a lower bound increasing 93.8% (95% CrI 36.4–186.4) in individuals aged 55–64 to 273.5% (95% CrI 167.8–423.4%) in individuals aged 45–54 when compared to the first wave (Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct statement of IFR increase with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The obtained lower bound for the overall IFR during the Gamma-dominated period in Manaus was 0.527% (95% CrI 0.447–0.630), 2.91 (95% CrI 2.43–3.53) times higher than the estimated IFR for the first wave in Manaus.
source: The obtained lower bound for the overall IFR was 0.527% (95% CrI 0.447–0.630), 2.91 (95% CrI 2.43–3.53) times higher than the estimated IFR for the first wave in Manaus.
evidence: Direct statement of overall IFR estimate and comparison from Results section.

claim: Blood donor-based serial cross-sectional serosurveillance recapitulates divergent epidemic dynamics across eight of Brazil's biggest cities.
source: Our results highlight the divergent epidemic dynamics across eight of Brazil's biggest cities as reflected by mortality rates, and show that these differences are recapitulated in blood donor-based serial cross-sectional serosurveillance.
evidence: Summary statement based on correlation between seroprevalence and mortality data.

claim: Blood donors are a convenient population for serosurveillance.
source: These results reinforce the validity of blood donors as a convenient population for serosurveillance.
evidence: Inference based on the strong correlation between seroprevalence and mortality.

claim: Blood donation programs are an existing component of medical infrastructure globally.
source: As blood donation programs are an existing component of medical infrastructure globally and in which blood samples are readily available in many locations, this approach can be rapidly implemented and carried out in large populations.
evidence: Statement based on general knowledge of healthcare infrastructure.

claim: Higher attack rates in individuals aged 16–54 years is consistent with previous work examining age patterns of transmission from mobility data in the United States.
source: We estimated larger attack rates in individuals aged 16–54 years. This is consistent with previous work examining age patterns of transmission from mobility data in the United States (Monod et al., 2021), but we have measured infection directly rather than making inferences indirectly on the basis of COVID-19 deaths and movement.
evidence: Comparison with published study on age-specific transmission patterns.

claim: Possible reasons for the higher attack rate in people aged 16–54 years include different risk perception and shielding practises, and disease biology with more frequent asymptomatic infections in younger people.
source: Possible reasons for the higher attack rate in people aged 16–54 years include, but are not limited to, different risk perception and shielding practises, and disease biology with more frequent asymptomatic infections in younger people, which increase infection risk in this age group due to greater mixing among working age adults.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed age patterns in seroprevalence.

claim: Heterogeneity in transmission in Manaus meant that some groups remained relatively susceptible and perpetuated transmission at a lower level.
source: This heterogeneity in transmission in a location with high overall antibody prevalence meant that some groups remained relatively susceptible and perpetuated transmission at a lower level (Buss and Sabino, 2021; Lalwani et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference about transmission dynamics supported by citations.

claim: Socioeconomic condition contributed to heterogeneity of SARS-CoV-2 spread in Manaus.
source: Other works suggest that socioeconomic condition also contributed to heterogeneity of SARS-CoV-2 spread in Manaus (Lalwani et al., 2021), which is confirmed by the large seroprevalence observed in Black and less-educated donors (Appendix 1—figure 20).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to data in Appendix figure.

claim: Large seroprevalence was observed in Black and less-educated donors in Manaus.
source: Other works suggest that socioeconomic condition also contributed to heterogeneity of SARS-CoV-2 spread in Manaus (Lalwani et al., 2021), which is confirmed by the large seroprevalence observed in Black and less-educated donors (Appendix 1—figure 20).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Appendix figure showing demographic patterns.

claim: The more affluent south and southeastern cities of Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, and São Paulo tended to have higher age-specific IFRs.
source: For example, the more affluent south and southeastern cities of Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, and São Paulo tended to have higher age-specific IFRs, whereas in the northern and northeastern cities of Manaus, Salvador, and Fortaleza, the age-specific IFRs tended to be lower.
evidence: Direct statement of geographic pattern in IFRs from Discussion section.

claim: In the northern and northeastern cities of Manaus, Salvador, and Fortaleza, the age-specific IFRs tended to be lower.
source: For example, the more affluent south and southeastern cities of Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, and São Paulo tended to have higher age-specific IFRs, whereas in the northern and northeastern cities of Manaus, Salvador, and Fortaleza, the age-specific IFRs tended to be lower.
evidence: Direct statement of geographic pattern in IFRs from Discussion section.

claim: Lower IFRs in northern and northeastern cities may reflect lower prevalence of comorbidities in those populations.
source: This may be due to under-reporting of deaths but might also reflect lower prevalence of comorbidities in the latter populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Speculative explanation for IFR differences with reference to comorbidity data.

claim: Cities with larger IFRs also had larger IHRs.
source: Cities with larger IFRs also had larger IHRs, suggesting that the differences in IFR reflect the different risks of developing a severe disease.
evidence: Direct statement based on comparison of IFR and IHR estimates.

claim: The differences in IFR reflect the different risks of developing a severe disease.
source: Cities with larger IFRs also had larger IHRs, suggesting that the differences in IFR reflect the different risks of developing a severe disease.
evidence: Inference based on correlation between IFR and IHR.

claim: The different lineages circulating in the eight cities may have contributed to the observed IFR and IHR difference.
source: The different lineages circulating in the eight cities may have also contributed to the observed IFR and IHR difference (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Speculative explanation with reference to lineage data in Appendix.

claim: The Gamma VOC tends to cause more severe disease than the ancestral non-Gamma variants circulating locally in Manaus.
source: Our results also clearly demonstrate a higher IHR during the Gamma-dominated observation period compared to the non-Gamma observation period in Manaus for all age groups (Figure 5). This supports observations (Banho et al., 2021) that the Gamma VOC tends to cause more severe disease than the ancestral non-Gamma variants circulating locally, even among young adults in Manaus.
evidence: Inference based on IHR comparison supported by citation.

claim: The larger increase in IHR for younger adults aged 25–54 years is compatible with the younger profile of hospitalisations of the Gamma-dominated wave in Brazil.
source: The larger increase in IHR for younger adults aged 25–54 years is compatible with the younger profile of hospitalisations of the Gamma-dominated wave in Brazil (de Souza et al., 2021), observed before vaccination coverage reached significant levels in older age groups.
evidence: Comparison with published observations on hospitalization patterns.

claim: The increased levels of hospitalisation caused parts of the healthcare system to collapse during the second wave in Manaus causing an increase in HFR.
source: In Manaus, the increased levels of hospitalisation caused parts of the healthcare system to collapse during the second wave causing an increase in HFR as previously described (Brizzi et al., 2021), further increasing the IFR.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published study on healthcare collapse.

claim: The higher IFR associated with Gamma VOC infection during the second wave is due to a combination of increased disease severity and the impacts of healthcare pressure on mortality within-hospitals.
source: The higher IFR associated with Gamma VOC infection during the second wave is therefore due to a combination of two factors – increased disease severity resulting in a greater proportion of infections requiring hospital-based care (the IHR, arising primarily from intrinsic viral properties and pathogenicity), and the impacts of this increased healthcare pressure on mortality within-hospitals (the HFR, arising primarily from healthcare pressure).
evidence: Inference based on decomposition of IFR into IHR and HFR components.

claim: Blood donors are limited to those aged 16–69 years in Brazil due to eligibility criteria.
source: Due to eligibility criteria in Brazil, blood donors are limited to those aged 16–69 years, with a strong skew towards younger adults even within this eligibility range (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) in most Brazilian regions.
evidence: Statement of blood donation eligibility criteria in Brazil.

claim: Blood donor serosurveillance agrees with other metrics of epidemic size as mortality, both cumulatively and through time.
source: However, our results do suggest that blood donor serosurveillance agrees with other metrics of epidemic size as mortality, both cumulatively (Figure 5B) and through time (Figure 3).
evidence: Inference based on correlation analyses shown in figures.

claim: Both sensitivity and seroreversion could be an age-dependent process as a proxy for disease severity.
source: Moreover, both sensitivity and seroreversion could be an age-dependent process as a proxy for disease severity, i.e., older individuals are more likely to be symptomatic, seroconvert, and have longer time to seroreversion.
evidence: Speculation about potential age-dependent antibody dynamics.

claim: Individuals that had a severe disease are unlikely to donate blood.
source: However, since individuals that had a severe disease are unlikely to donate blood, seropositive whole blood donors are likely fairly homogenous in having had milder or asymptomatic disease, and as such, the rate of waning may not vary significantly between locations.
evidence: Inference based on blood donation eligibility criteria.

claim: Seropositive whole blood donors are likely fairly homogenous in having had milder or asymptomatic disease.
source: However, since individuals that had a severe disease are unlikely to donate blood, seropositive whole blood donors are likely fairly homogenous in having had milder or asymptomatic disease, and as such, the rate of waning may not vary significantly between locations.
evidence: Inference based on blood donation eligibility criteria.

claim: The model produces upper bounds for cumulative prevalence of >100% in Manaus by early 2021 due to reinfections.
source: For this reason, our model produces upper bounds for cumulative prevalence of >100% in Manaus by early 2021.
evidence: Direct statement explaining model output in context of reinfections.

claim: Blood donors represent an accessible population to detect trends of the epidemic that otherwise could only be obtained through expensive population-based studies.
source: Despite these limitations, blood donors represent an accessible population to detect trends of the epidemic that otherwise could only be obtained through expensive population-based studies, which are difficult to establish in Brazil during the course of a rapidly progressing epidemic.
evidence: Inference about the practical utility of blood donor surveillance.
